summary: Updates the IANA registration procedures for H.248/MEGACO packages. It describes the process more clearly and sets up a more formal review and feedback step. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Before a new item goes on a list, a few people check it. This writes down the checking steps for an official list used by phone-gateway equipment.

questions: what is an h.248 megaco package
how to register a megaco package with iana
what is the iesg expert reviewer
what is the difference between in progress and final package status
subtitle: How new H.248/MEGACO packages, error codes, reasons and profile names get reviewed before IANA records them.

tldr.problem: H.248/MEGACO packages were registered with IANA without an in-depth expert review, so some were not fully aligned with H.248/MEGACO principles and were hard to fix once published.
tldr.mechanism: IANA forwards each public registration request to an IESG-appointed expert, who checks it against the package template, protocol syntax and existing work before telling IANA to register it.
tldr.outcome: Packages stay at status IP (In Progress) until they have been reviewed and found acceptable, and only then can move to Final. Error codes, ServiceChange reasons and profile names follow similar expert-reviewed procedures.

facts.label: Package name length
facts.value: A letter plus up to 63 letters, digits or underscores

facts.label: Error text and reason text limit

today: RFC 5615 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 151). The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the published description of the H.248/MEGACO registration review process.

sections.title: Why the Old Process Needed Fixing
sections.content:
H.248/MEGACO lets other organizations define Packages: bundles that let a new function be controlled through the protocol. The idea was that groups with deep knowledge of one area could write their own, because neither the IETF MEGACO Working Group nor ITU-T Study Group 16 knew every area.

This worked in the number and range of Packages produced, but some were not fully aligned with H.248/MEGACO principles, and once a Package is published and registered it is hard to correct. The IANA process never required an in-depth review. Earlier, the MEGACO Working Group chair acted as the IESG-appointed expert and gave Packages an informal review. That group has since disbanded, and new work typically happens in Question 3 of ITU-T Study Group 16.
sections.eli5: Lots of different groups made add-on parts for the same system, and nobody was checking them carefully. Some did not fit well, and they were hard to fix after being shared.

sections.title: Package Name Syntax
sections.content: Text-encoded PackageIDs must follow the PackageName encoding in H.248.1 Annex B, which the RFC repeats in ABNF: NAME = ALPHA *63(ALPHA / DIGIT / "_"). A name is a letter followed by up to 63 more letters, digits or underscores, and a digit is not allowed as the first character.
sections.eli5: A package name is like a username: it has to start with a letter, and after that it can use letters, numbers and underscores.

sections.title: The Package Registration Procedure
sections.content:
Registering a public Package is "specification required" as defined in RFC 5226. Requesters are encouraged to register early to reserve a binary ID, to check their work against the Package Definition section of H.248.1, and to send it to the ITU-T Question responsible for H.248 (Q.3/16 at the time of writing). Private Packages do not need a specification, though one is encouraged.

When IANA receives an initial or final request, it forwards it to the IESG-appointed expert. The expert compares the Package with the template, protocol syntax and procedures, checks that it does not duplicate existing functionality and that security issues are addressed, and works with the requester to resolve problems. If the Package is suitable, the expert issues an approval statement, copied to IANA.

Status IP
In Progress: not fully reviewed and approved, so it may contain errors or be inconsistent with H.248 principles. New Packages start here.
Status Final
Reviewed, approved and stable. The status stays IP if the Package was not provided for review or has outstanding comments.
sections.eli5: You hand in your new part, a checker compares it with the rules and with what already exists, and only when it passes does it get marked as finished.

sections.title: What the Expert Checks for a Package
sections.content:
The expert makes sure that each Package has a unique string name, a unique serial number and a version number. The string name is the PackageID for text encoding and the serial number is the PackageID for binary encoding. Public Packages MUST get serial numbers from 0x0001 to 0x7fff, private ones from 0x8000 to 0xffff, and serial number 0 is reserved.

  • The requester gives a contact name with an email and postal address.
  • A public Package needs a reference to a document that states the version it describes. If that document is not public, it must be available to the expert without a non-disclosure agreement.
  • Packages registered by other than recognized standards bodies need a name of at least 8 characters.
  • Names are first-come, first-served if all other conditions are met.
sections.eli5: Each part needs its own name and number, a person to contact, and a written description. Names are given out in the order people ask.

sections.title: Error Codes, Reasons and Profile Names
sections.content:
Three other registries get their own procedures, included for completeness and to make the reviewer's role explicit.

  • Error Codes: an error number and a one-line string of at most 80 characters, with a public description clear enough to tell it apart from all other codes. Standards bodies get 3- or 4-character error numbers; everyone else gets 4-character ones. Only the original definer can modify a definition, and a change to the number, name or string is treated as a new request with Expert Review.
  • ServiceChange Reasons: a reason number and a unique one-phrase string of at most 80 characters, with a public description that distinguishes it from all other reasons.
  • Profile Names: a unique name and version (the version may be omitted when the name has a wildcard), plus contact details. Non-standards bodies need at least 6 characters. A name ending in the wildcard asterisk at the end is accepted if the first 6 characters are fully specified, and IANA issues no other names in that range.
sections.eli5: Other lists, like error numbers and profile names, get the same kind of check. Each entry must be clearly different from the rest and have a written explanation.

sections.title: What IANA Records
sections.content:
IANA forwards each request to the IESG-appointed expert and registers it only when the expert says so. For a Package it records the serial number (binary ID), text name, version, extension information, status (IP or Final), and the name, reference and contact. Packages are listed in increasing order of serial number, and the latest version replaces the previous one. IANA assigns serial numbers in consecutive order of registration, except that an update keeps the existing number.

The RFC does not alter the tabular Package, Error Code and ServiceChange Reason information already in the registry.
sections.eli5: The record keeper writes the new entry in the list only after the checker says yes, and keeps the list in number order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the new procedures have no additional security implications. Packages work inside the framework of the core H.248.1 specification and cannot update it. A Media Gateway Controller and a Media Gateway act only on elements they know, and answer an unknown PackageID with an error inside their control association.

A malicious Package would be unlikely to cause problems: if only one side implemented it, the other would not understand or never request it. Requesters and the Expert Reviewer should still check that a Package adds no security issues, and a requester for a public Package must be authorized by its standards organization.
sections.eli5: A fake part would not work because the other side would not know what to do with it and would just say no.
